sources.entry: The Shape and Feel of the Post-AI Data Stack

summary.title: The Shape and Feel of the Post-AI Data Stack
summary.one_liner: Learn how data teams shift from producing analyses to engineering company-wide consensus, using agent-readable artifacts, agent-operable tools, semantic layers, and evals, drawing on Ian Macomber's experience at Wayfair and Ramp.
takeaways: AI makes producing analysis cheap, so the scarce resource for data teams becomes company-wide agreement on metric definitions and reality.
Make data outputs machine-readable (e.g. per-dashboard llms.txt, markdown descriptors, fetchable SQL) so agents can find and reassemble them.
Test consensus by asking the same metric question across every interface and model combination, and track consensus divergence rate; it should be zero for board-level metrics.
Evaluate both the final answer and the evidence path (which docs, semantic views, and queries were used), and fix failures by improving context rather than waiting for better models.
Keep semantic layers and business context portable and headless across tools, and handle unstructured data by running versioned AI tagging offline and writing back structured fields.
summary.summary: The author traces data stack evolution from his time at Wayfair (on-prem SQL Server, ~2013) through cloud warehouses (~2016) and the Modern Data Stack with reverse ETL (~2020), arguing each shift expanded what a data scientist could do. He then describes the post-AI era (~2026), where data teams must enable everyone to build with data and own a single agreed-upon version of reality. Requirements covered include agent-readable artifacts, agent-operable and agent-agnostic tooling, and engineered consensus measured through repeated cross-interface question tests and evals. The post is grounded in examples from Ramp's internal BI tool and research agent, including trace-based eval design and a versioned AI tagger for Gong calls.
